claim: Degree distributions in protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks are believed to follow a power law (PL).
source_text: Degree distributions in protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks are believed to follow a power law (PL).
evidence_reasoning: This statement reflects established belief in the field, presented as existing scientific consensus.

claim: Technical and study bias affect the experimental procedures for detecting PPIs.
source_text: However, technical and study bias affect the experimental procedures for detecting PPIs.
evidence_reasoning: This is presented as an established fact about experimental limitations in PPI detection.

claim: Cancer-associated proteins have received disproportional attention.
source_text: For instance, cancer-associated proteins have received disproportional attention.
evidence_reasoning: This is stated as a known example of study bias in the field.

claim: Bait proteins in large-scale experiments tend to have many false-positive interaction partners.
source_text: Moreover, bait proteins in large-scale experiments tend to have many false-positive interaction partners.
evidence_reasoning: This is presented as an established characteristic of technical bias in large-scale PPI experiments.

claim: The authors studied the degree distributions of thousands of PPI networks of controlled provenance.
source_text: Studying the degree distributions of thousands of PPI networks of controlled provenance, we address the question if PL distributions in observed PPI networks could be explained by these biases alone.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study, indicating data collection and analysis.

claim: Study bias and technical bias suffice to produce the observed PL distribution in PPI networks.
source_text: Our findings are supported by mathematical models and extensive simulations and indicate that study bias and technical bias suffice to produce the observed PL distribution.
evidence_reasoning: This is the main finding of the study, supported by mathematical models and simulations (data), and represents an inference from the analysis.

claim: The findings are supported by mathematical models and extensive simulations.
source_text: Our findings are supported by mathematical models and extensive simulations
evidence_reasoning: This explicitly states that mathematical models and simulations were used as supporting evidence.

claim: It is problematic to derive hypotheses about the topology of the true biological interactome from the PL distributions in observed PPI networks.
source_text: It is, hence, problematic to derive hypotheses about the topology of the true biological interactome from the PL distributions in observed PPI networks.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion inferred from the finding that biases can produce PL distributions.

claim: The study casts doubt on the use of the PL property of biological networks as a modeling assumption or quality criterion in network biology.
source_text: Our study casts doubt on the use of the PL property of biological networks as a modeling assumption or quality criterion in network biology.
evidence_reasoning: This is an implication drawn from the study's findings about the artifactual nature of PL distributions.

claim: PL distributions in observed PPI networks could potentially be explained by study bias and technical bias alone.
source_text: we address the question if PL distributions in observed PPI networks could be explained by these biases alone.
evidence_reasoning: This is the research question that the study addresses through data analysis and inference.

claim: The observed PL distributions in PPI networks may not reflect the true topology of the biological interactome.
source_text: It is, hence, problematic to derive hypotheses about the topology of the true biological interactome from the PL distributions in observed PPI networks.
evidence_reasoning: This is logically implied by the statement that it is problematic to derive hypotheses about true topology from observed PL distributions.
